claims.text: The selected equiatomic Nb-Ti-V high-entropy alloy is chemically and structurally homogeneous as synthesized.
Superconductivity in the selected Nb-Ti-V alloy is governed primarily by electron-phonon coupling.
Isotopic substitution of a constituent element can alter the alloy's phonon spectrum through the change in atomic mass.
In conventional BCS superconductivity, electron-phonon coupling mediates superconducting pairing.
Changing the isotopic mass of one element changes its vibrational frequencies.
The isotope-induced change in the phonon spectrum modifies the electron-phonon interaction strength.
The superconducting transition temperature should typically scale as the inverse square root of the relevant isotopic mass.
Increasing the isotopic mass of Ti should lower the associated phonon frequencies.
Increasing the isotopic mass should reduce Tc relative to the natural-isotope baseline.
The reduction in Tc should be consistent with inverse-square-root mass scaling.
Failure to observe the predicted isotope shift would indicate that mechanisms other than electron-phonon coupling may dominate.
The isotope-effect hypothesis applies only while the alloy remains compositionally uniform and is adequately described by conventional BCS-type pairing.
Disorder introduced by isotope substitution could independently affect Tc and confound the proposed test.
Interactions involving other constituents in a multicomponent HEA may partially mask the isotope effect.
An Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy family contains a superconducting bcc phase close to a weak-coupling, BCS-type phonon-mediated superconductor.
Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08 is a type-II HEA superconductor with Tc near 7.5 K and intermediate electron-phonon coupling.

No significant Tc shift after confirmed isotope substitution and preservation of stoichiometry would falsify the hypothesis that superconductivity is governed predominantly by electron-phonon coupling.
